newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS-Danish, Swedish bourses to merge trading.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Danish, Swedish bourses to merge trading.

text.p: The Copenhagen and Stockholm stock exchanges on Thursday announced plans to merge trading, a move that they hope will boost the combined bourses' turnover by at least 10 percent and act as the first step toward a pan-Nordic securities market.

Speaking at a news conference in the Danish capital, local bourse president Lars Johansen said that a joint share-trading system should be operating between summer of 1998 and 1999 depending on the technical system chosen.

"Our prime goal is to make the Nordic market more interesting than it is today and make it easier for large institutional clients from outside the Nordic region to come in and trade Nordic securities," he said.
Depending on the results of the joint share-trading operation a bond-trading alliance would be introduced a year or two later, he added.
"As the market will be more attractive and easier we expect more trade. We reckon that more players will come to the market and trade more," Swedish exchange president Bengt Ryden said.
Neither man would put a figure on the expected increase but Johansen said they were thinking in terms of double-digit growth.

He said a joint company, Nordic Exchanges (NOX) would be formed to handle marketing and sales. The new firm, to be owned 50-50 by the two bourses, would be based in Copenhagen and could open offices in Stockholm and London.
A joint NOX share index was a possibility for the future, Johansen added, as was a Nordic blue-chip index.
No cross-ownership between the parent companies was seen at the moment, Copenhagen bourse chairman Hans Ejvind Hansen said after the news conference.
"Not at this stage. We never know what will happen in the future but we have no plans in that direction," he told Reuters.
Johansen said that the new partners had invited the Finnish, Icelandic and Norwegian bourses to join the alliance but Helsinki and Oslo had already chosen new trading systems.
"They must now evaluate the situation, now and in the next year or two, and decide if they want to join us," he said.

"The alliance between Stockholm and Copenhagen is a breakthrough in the quest to create an integrated Nordic securities market...We hope that other Nordic exchanges will join," a joint statement from Johansen and Ryden said.
Finland and Norway, however, are reluctant to join a system they see as dominated by Stockholm, by far the largest stock market in the region.

In the Copenhagen-Stockholm system each exchange will remain independent and retain responsibility for listing companies and supervising trading and membership but rules and regulations will be gradually harmonised.
Share trading will be done over the Stockholm Stock Exchange's SAX system, either the existing SAX 1, or the updated SAX 2000 which would take longer to implement.
Membership and operating costs for the combined market would be cheaper than for the two individually and administration simpler, the statement said.
Swedish 1996 share turnover was 918 billion Swedish crowns ($118.5 billion), while Copenhagen's volume was 217 billion Danish crowns ($33 billion).
